body: Interesting problem. Of course, a normal user is normally not allowed to create or rename files in `/dev` so this is a bit niche.

The current method is done to make sure the creation of the file is atomic when multiple processes write to the same file.

What's the correct fix to avoid this issue? Avoid the rename dance if the target file is not a normal file?

> ...
> What's the correct fix to avoid this issue? Avoid the rename dance if the target file is not a normal file?

if you want atomic creation then O_CREAT|O_EXCL should give it to you but won't work with character special devices. to get consistent behaviour you'd have to use just O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW, then acquire an advisory lock, then fstat() and if S_ISREG() call ftruncate(). there are a _lot_ of security implications around this dance.

On Sun, Apr 11, 2021 at 02:22:12AM -0700, rofl0r wrote:
> ...
> read cookies: open(filename, O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC), read() ; close();
> write cookies:
> open(filename, O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC|O_CLOEXEC, 0660); write(); close();
> ...

i strongly suggest O_NOFOLLOW in both cases.

> in case you want to avoid to lose content written by other curl
> processes, the write step could maybe use O_APPEND instead of O_WRONLY etc.

unless we can define the cooperation model among multiple processes and
ensure that all write()'s are atomic (so, no stdio here), i suggest the
use of advisory locking to either force a delay until the existing process
is complete or induce failure if there's already some process with an open().

-- 
Paul Vixie
Why isn't it enough to just check if it's a device beforehand? Do we really need to deal with devices atomically?

On Sun, Apr 11, 2021 at 09:35:10PM -0700, Jay Satiro wrote:
> Why isn't it enough to just check if it's a device beforehand?
> Do we really need to deal with devices atomically?

if we had a red team they might say there are too many what-ifs
like a path-intermediate symlink changing where it points between
the stat() and later open(). if you open() it first and then
fstat() it there's not a lot that can go wrong. what would be the
advantage of a non-atomic approach?

-- 
Paul Vixie

In [cookie_output](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/curl-7_76_0/lib/cookie.c#L1540-L1551) you can see that it uses fopen to create a temporary file and then rename to rename it. What I wanted to know is why we can't just check that if target already exists that it's normal and can be replaced. I wonder why rename was used instead of open O_CREAT O_EXCL like we already do in [tool_create_output_file](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/curl-7_76_0/src/tool_cb_wrt.c#L78) which is used elsewhere.

edit: tool_create_output_file uses fopen too, excl only used to prevent overwrite. I had thought unlink... open excl... which would give the same result but still the problem of unlinking /dev/null

> why rename was used instead of open O_CREAT O_EXCL

No good reason I think. And as mentioned in here, it should be changed...
Well, maybe the fact that `O_EXCL` would change behavior slightly as it would rather make the saving fail rather than overwriting an existing file.

> No good reason I think. And as mentioned in here, it should be changed...

I edited right as you posted. It appears that there's still the same issue. In other words,

fopen temp file
rename temp file -> target

or

unlink target
open excl target

either way it's the same problem where we don't have an atomic way to figure out if it's a device when we unlink  or rename

On Mon, Apr 12, 2021 at 12:28:01AM -0700, Jay Satiro wrote:
> ...or
> 
> unlink target
> open excl target
> 
> either way it's the same problem where we don't have an atomic way
> to figure out if it's a device when we unlink  or rename

this is i think why openat(), unlinkat(), and renameat() were created.
by trimming off the final pathname component and opendir()'ing what's
left, it's possible to avoid the impact of any changes to any interior
symlink in the pathname. under those conditions, if lstat() says that
the final filename (possible target of renameat()) is not a regular
file (so, directory or symlink or device node) then it's safe to fail
and if it is a regular file it's safe to do a renameat().

so, not atomic, but the remaining race condition is that a direntry
that was a regular file one syscall ago has changed to a device node
before the renameat(). i realize that curl (or libcurl) can execute as
root and so stomping /dev/null remains a theoretical possibility. but
unless you're willing to do what some text editors now do, this is "it".

editors, because of symlinks, are sometimes made to copy out the old
file to a backup file, then export the content to the old file, all
without creating or renaming anything. if curl wants to do that with
its cookie jar i don't think there will be complaints.

my recommendation for advisory locking stands, though, in case of multiple
jobs updating the same cookie jar simultaneously. that's not an "atomics"
problem, rather it's a problem caused by some (any?) solutions to the
"atomics" problem.

-- 
Paul Vixie

> my recommendation for advisory locking stands, though, in case of multiple jobs updating the same cookie jar simultaneously

This does indeed seem like the most sensible approach that should work with regular files and character devices alike.

The alt-svc and HSTS saving code also have the same flaw as they work the same way as the cookie save.

issue.title: lib: when saving files, use advisory locks

body:
On Mon, Apr 12, 2021 at 04:52:24AM -0700, Daniel Stenberg wrote:
> > my recommendation for advisory locking stands, though, in case of multiple jobs updating the same cookie jar simultaneously
> 
> This does indeed seem like the most sensible approach that should work with regular files and character devices alike.

i worry about the portability layer; vax/vms and ms-dos for example don't have the open() options needed for this.

> The alt-svc and HSTS saving code also have the same flaw as they work the same way as the cookie save.

i can propose a fix if you wish.
I started an attempt to use locking instead of rename over in #6884
I've not been able to create a fix that doesn't just create another issue (race condition). This issue thus remains.

would you mind sharing the roads you tried that went nowhere?

-- 
Paul Vixie

The current operation (that this issue refers to) makes one out of multiple processes always successfully write the whole file (and it potentially overwrites the others') since it uses rename at the end of the save.

I have not been able to do open+lock in a way that works that way without a race condition because I need to do open and lock in two separate non-atomic operations!

What semantics do you want for the cookie jar exactly?

If you want to keep the current semantics (one process wins, overwriting all the other changes), it can be achieved with a
sequence of open, blocking lock, write all you need, ftruncate to the current size, close (which unlocks). It does not matter if several processes open the file at the same time: all but one will block on the lock, and the last one to unblock will "win" because it will write() and ftruncate() last.

On Mon, May 03, 2021 at 08:35:47AM -0700, Laurent Bercot wrote:
> If you want to keep the current semantics (one process wins, overwriting all the other changes), it can be achieved with a
> sequence of open, blocking lock, write all you need, ftruncate to the current size, close (which unlocks). It does not matter if several processes open the file at the same time: all but one will block on the lock, and the last one to unblock will "win" because it will write() and ftruncate() last.

+1.

-- 
Paul Vixie
